Specific Heat Capacity Formula: Q = mcΔT
The specific heat capacity equation Q = mcΔT tells you exactly how much energy is needed to heat any material. It explains why metals heat up quickly, why water heats slowly, and why the oceans moderate Earth's climate.

Think of it as a thermal bucket: a wide bucket (high c) needs more water poured in (more energy) to raise the water level (temperature) by the same amount as a narrow bucket (low c).

Engine cooling systems

results.title: Understanding the Specific Heat Capacity Equation: A Guide
excerpts:
Specific heat capacity, usually written as (c), is a material property. A material with a high specific heat capacity needs more energy for the same temperature rise. Water is a common example: it takes much more energy to heat water than the same mass of many metals by the same temperature difference.
The specific heat capacity formula
The most common engineering form of the specific heat capacity equation is:
$$ Q = mc\Delta T $$
This equation says that heat energy (Q) increases in direct proportion to mass (m), specific heat capacity (c), and temperature change (\Delta T). If any one of those three terms doubles while the others stay the same, the required heat energy doubles.
* (\Delta T) | Temperature change | K or °C difference | °F difference | Use a temperature difference, not an absolute temperature value.
Rule of thumb
Water has a high specific heat capacity, about (4.18,\text{kJ/(kg·K)}). Heating (1,\text{kg}) of water by (10^\circ\text{C}) takes about (41.8,\text{kJ}).

Calorimetry, Explained (Q = mcΔT)
After reading this you can compute the heat needed to warm or cool any object, and rearrange Q = mc\Delta T to solve for mass, specific heat, or temperature change with real units.
What Q = mcΔT tells you
Q = m , c , \Delta T
Read each symbol carefully:
Q Heat energy transferred, in joules (J). Positive when heat flows into the object, negative when heat flows out. m Mass of the substance, in grams (g) when c is in J/g·°C. c Specific heat: the energy needed to raise 1 g by 1 °C. It is a fixed property of the material.
Worked example: heating 500 g of water by 20 °C
These are the demo defaults: water, mass 500 g , temperature change 20 °C , solving for heat.
With mass fixed at 500 g and ΔT at 20 °C, the heat required is directly proportional to specific heat: water at 4.186 J/g·°C needs 41,860 J, while copper at 0.385 J/g·°C needs only 3,850 J, a factor of about 10.9 less.
The sign of Q carries physical meaning. If you solve with a negative \Delta T (cooling), Q comes out negative, meaning the object releases that much heat. Cooling 500 g of water from 40 °C to 20 °C gives \Delta T = -20 °C and Q = -41{,}860 J: the water sheds 41.86 kJ into its surroundings.
